question: In which hill fort was Shivaji, the founder of the Maratha power, born in 1630?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shivneri.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shivaji was born in 1630 at the fort of Shivneri, near Junnar in present-day Pune district of Maharashtra, and was named after the local goddess Shivai Devi of the Shivneri temple (शिवाजी का जन्म 1630 में शिवनेरी दुर्ग में हुआ)

 

• His father Shahaji Bhosale served the Deccan sultanates, while his mother Jijabai shaped his early outlook and values.

 

• Shivneri is therefore the birthplace, whereas the other forts named became important at later stages of his career as a capital, a conquest or a battle site.

 

• Shivneri stands near Junnar in the Pune region, on the western edge of the Deccan plateau, and its steep rock faces made it a formidable fort even before Shivaji's lifetime.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shivaji's first major conquest is traditionally taken to be the fort of Torna, captured around 1646-47 from Bijapur.

 

• Raigad was made the capital in the 1670s and hosted the coronation of 1674.

 

• Pratapgad fort is linked with the 1659 episode involving the Bijapuri general Afzal Khan.

 

• Shivneri is today maintained as a preserved monument, and a small shrine to Shivai Devi stands within it.

 

NOTE

 

• Raigad (Option 1): Raigad was developed as the Maratha capital and hosted the 1674 coronation, but it was not where Shivaji was born; the birth took place at a different hill fort near Junnar.

 

• Torna (Option 2): Torna was the first fort Shivaji captured from Bijapur in his early youth, which makes it a milestone of his rise, not the place of his birth in 1630.

 

• Pratapgad (Option 4): Pratapgad was built by Shivaji near Mahabaleshwar and is famous for the 1659 clash with Afzal Khan, so it belongs to his later career rather than his birth.

question: Who were the parents of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shahaji and Jijabai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shivaji was the son of Shahaji Bhosale, a Maratha noble serving the Deccan sultanates, and Jijabai, daughter of the Jadhav family of Sindkhed (शिवाजी के माता-पिता शाहजी भोंसले और जीजाबाई थे)

 

• Jijabai is remembered for instilling courage and a sense of Hindu self-rule in the young Shivaji, who grew up largely around Pune.

 

• Dadoji Konddev was only the guardian-administrator of Shahaji's Pune jagir, and Sambhaji was Shivaji's own son, so neither can be a parent.

 

• Because Shahaji was often posted away on Bijapur's campaigns in the south, Jijabai took responsibility for the boy's upbringing at Pune, telling him stories from the epics that shaped his ideals.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shahaji held a jagir around Pune and later served Bijapur in the Karnataka region.

 

• Saibai was Shivaji's first wife and the mother of Sambhaji.

 

• Shivaji's son Sambhaji succeeded him in 1680.

 

• Shahaji Bhosale himself died around 1664 after a hunting accident in the Karnataka region.

 

• Shivaji's early training in administration came under Dadoji Konddev, who managed the family jagir at Pune and introduced revenue reforms in the area.

 

NOTE

 

• Shahaji and Saibai (Option 1): Saibai was the wife of Shivaji and the mother of his eldest son Sambhaji; she was not his mother, so pairing her with Shahaji gives a wrong parentage.

 

• Sambhaji and Jijabai (Option 2): Sambhaji was Shivaji's son and successor, born in 1657, so naming him as a father reverses the generations; Shivaji's father was Shahaji Bhosale.

 

• Dadoji Konddev and Jijabai (Option 3): Dadoji Konddev was the capable steward appointed by Shahaji to manage the Pune jagir and tutor Shivaji, so he was a mentor and not a parent.

question: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigarh fort in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1674.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In June 1674 Shivaji was formally crowned Chhatrapati at Raigarh fort, with the Vedic rites performed by the learned Brahmin Gaga Bhatt (1674 में रायगढ़ में शिवाजी का राज्याभिषेक)

 

• The ceremony gave legitimacy to his independent sovereign state, which rivalled the Mughals and the Deccan sultanates.

 

• Raigarh was afterwards made the capital of the Maratha kingdom.

 

• The year 1680, by contrast, marks his death, and not any coronation.

 

• Before this ceremony he was only a Maratha noble in the eyes of orthodox opinion, so the Vedic rites placed him formally among the ruling Kshatriya order and gave his kingdom a legal and religious status.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gaga Bhatt of Varanasi presided over the coronation ceremony.

 

• A second, Tantric-style coronation was reportedly held later in 1674 as well.

 

• Shivaji assumed the title Haindava Dharmoddharak among other titles.

 

• Rajaram, Sambhaji and later Maratha rulers carried forward the Chhatrapati title that Shivaji adopted in 1674.

 

• The title Chhatrapati literally means lord of the umbrella, which was a traditional symbol of sovereignty in Indian kingship.

 

NOTE

 

• 1664 (Option 1): The year 1664 falls in the period of Shivaji's clashes with Mughal governors, a decade before he was formally enthroned; no coronation took place then.

 

• 1670 (Option 3): A date of 1670 is associated with his second sack of Surat, a raid on a Mughal port city, not with enthronement at Raigarh fort.

 

• 1680 (Option 4): The year 1680 is when Shivaji died of fever, which triggered the succession dispute between his sons, so it cannot be the date of his coronation.

question: Which military strategy was Shivaji most famous for mastering and using against his stronger opponents?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Guerrilla warfare.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shivaji perfected guerrilla warfare, called Ganimi Kava in Marathi, using surprise raids, quick withdrawals and the rugged Western Ghats terrain against bigger armies (शिवाजी की गनिमी कावा या छापामार युद्ध नीति)

 

• Light, mobile infantry and cavalry could strike Mughal and Bijapuri forces and then vanish into hills and forts.

 

• Fixed battles in open fields would have favoured the numerically superior and better-equipped Mughal cavalry.

 

• The Maratha success lay in avoiding frontal battles with the heavier imperial cavalry, since a quick strike on supply lines and outposts could wear down an enemy army far larger than his own.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mountain forts acted as bases, storehouses and refuges for the Maratha raiders.

 

• Shivaji also built a navy on the Konkan coast, but it was not the basis of his land victories.

 

• Spies and a strong intelligence network supported the surprise attacks.

 

• Ganimi means enemy and Kava means stratagem or trick in the Marathi language.

 

NOTE

 

• Siege tactics with heavy artillery (Option 2): Heavy artillery sieges were a strength of the Mughal army with its large gun parks, whereas Shivaji, with limited resources, avoided such costly set-piece operations.

 

• Open field cavalry charges (Option 3): Open-field cavalry charges would have exposed his smaller force to the larger Mughal mansabdari cavalry, so he avoided them and preferred ambush and mobility in hilly country.

 

• Large-scale naval bombardment (Option 4): Shivaji did raise a Konkan navy, yet naval bombardment was never the core of his success against the Mughals; his fame rests on hill-based mobile land warfare.

question: Raja Jai Singh of Amber was sent by Aurangzeb against Shivaji after which Mughal governor of the Deccan had been defeated by the Marathas?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shaista Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aurangzeb first sent Shaista Khan, the Mughal governor of the Deccan, against Shivaji, but he was defeated by the Marathas (शाइस्ता खां मुगल दक्कन का सूबेदार था जिसे शिवाजी ने हराया)

 

• When this failed, Aurangzeb chose the experienced Rajput general Raja Jai Singh of Amber to crush Shivaji.

 

• Jai Singh made elaborate preparations and besieged the Purandar fort, forcing the Treaty of Purandar in 1665.

 

• Shaista Khan, who was a maternal uncle of Aurangzeb, had been sent to the Deccan to capture Maratha forts, and his defeat showed that the Mughals could not easily subdue Shivaji's hill country.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shaista Khan was Aurangzeb's maternal uncle.

 

• He was attacked in his residence at Pune in 1663 in a daring night raid.

 

• Jai Singh I served three Mughal emperors, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb.

 

• After Jai Singh's task of 1665, the Mughal command in the Deccan passed to Prince Muazzam and later to others.

 

NOTE

 

• Afzal Khan (Option 1): Afzal Khan was a general of the Adil Shahi sultanate of Bijapur, not a Mughal governor of the Deccan; he was killed by Shivaji at Pratapgad in 1659.

 

• Mirza Raja Man Singh (Option 2): Man Singh was an Amber ruler under Akbar in the sixteenth century, far earlier than Aurangzeb's reign, and he had nothing to do with the Deccan governorship in the 1660s.

 

• Diler Khan (Option 4): Diler Khan was a Mughal officer who accompanied Jai Singh on the Purandar campaign, but he was not the governor whose defeat led to Jai Singh's deployment.

question: The Treaty of Purandar (1665) was concluded between Shivaji and which Mughal commander?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Raja Jai Singh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Purandar was signed in 1665 between Shivaji and the Mughal general Raja Jai Singh of Amber, after Jai Singh besieged Purandar fort (1665 की पुरंदर की संधि शिवाजी और जयसिंह के बीच हुई)

 

• Shivaji had lodged his family and treasure in the Purandar fort, so its siege forced him to open negotiations.

 

• Jai Singh acted on behalf of Emperor Aurangzeb, who wanted to curb the rising Maratha power.

 

• The treaty marked a temporary submission of Shivaji to the Mughal power, since a ruler who had defied Aurangzeb now agreed to hold his remaining territory as a Mughal-linked noble.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mirza Raja Jai Singh was a Kachhwaha Rajput ruler of Amber.

 

• The treaty is sometimes counted among the early confrontations of Aurangzeb with Maratha power.

 

• Purandar fort lies near Pune in the Western Ghats.

 

• Jai Singh also fought Bijapur in 1665-66 and failed to take it, which strained his standing with Aurangzeb.

 

NOTE

 

• Shaista Khan (Option 2): Shaista Khan had already been humiliated by Shivaji before the treaty and was replaced in the Deccan operation; he did not negotiate the terms of 1665.

 

• Afzal Khan (Option 3): Afzal Khan served Bijapur and was killed in 1659, six years before the treaty, so he could not have been a signatory on the Mughal side.

 

• Mahabat Khan (Option 4): Mahabat Khan was a noble of Jahangir and Shah Jahan who died in the 1630s, long before Shivaji began to confront the Mughals in this manner.

question: Under the Treaty of Purandar, how many of his forts did Shivaji surrender to the Mughals?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 23 of 35.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• By the Treaty of Purandar Shivaji agreed to surrender 23 of his 35 forts to the Mughals (पुरंदर संधि में शिवाजी ने 35 में से 23 किले मुगलों को सौंपे)

 

• The remaining 12 forts were left with him, on the condition that he remained loyal to the Mughal court.

 

• His son was also to serve the Mughal court as a mansabdar, which tied the Marathas to imperial service.

 

• Surrender of the larger share of forts deprived Shivaji of the strongholds that formed the military base of his kingdom, which explains why the treaty is counted as a major reverse for him.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shivaji agreed to help the Mughals against Bijapur in return.

 

• His young son Sambhaji was given a mansab of 5000 as per the arrangement.

 

• The treaty lasted only until his journey to Agra in 1666 broke the understanding.

 

• The forts given up included Purandar and several other strongholds near Pune.

 

NOTE

 

• 12 of 35 (Option 1): Twelve is the number of forts that Shivaji was allowed to keep, so choosing it reverses the figures by treating the retained forts as those surrendered.

 

• 35 of 35 (Option 2): Thirty-five is the total number of forts held by Shivaji, and surrendering all of them would have ended his power altogether, which the terms did not require.

 

• 17 of 35 (Option 3): Seventeen does not correspond to any figure in the treaty; the division was 23 forts handed over and 12 retained, as the Mughals sought partial, not equal, concessions.

question: Shivaji visited Aurangzeb's court at Agra in 1666, where he was insulted and held captive. Which of the following is correct regarding this episode?
option_1: He accepted the Treaty of Purandar after the humiliation
option_2: He refused to accept the Treaty of Purandar after being held captive
option_3: He was appointed governor of the Deccan
option_4: He was crowned Chhatrapati at Agra fort
solution_text:
The correct answer is He refused to accept the Treaty of Purandar after being held captive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In 1666 Shivaji went to the Mughal court at Agra Fort, was made to wait among lesser nobles and was kept under watch, and after this insult he refused to accept the Treaty of Purandar (आगरा दरबार में अपमान के बाद शिवाजी ने संधि मानने से इनकार किया)

 

• He later escaped from Agra, reportedly in baskets of sweets, and returned to Maharashtra to resume his campaigns.

 

• The episode ended the temporary peace of 1665 and renewed Maratha-Mughal hostility.

 

• The Agra visit was supposed to settle relations after the treaty, but Aurangzeb's court treated him as a petty chieftain, and the refusal that followed reopened the conflict that the treaty had paused.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shivaji is said to have escaped in August 1666.

 

• He reached Maharashtra in disguise as a sadhu.

 

• In 1670 he again raided Surat and recovered many of the forts ceded earlier.

 

• Aurangzeb was celebrating his fiftieth lunar birthday at court when the audience took place.

 

• Shivaji's departure from Agra is celebrated as one of the boldest escapes in Indian history, and after returning he soon renewed his raids on Mughal territory.

 

NOTE

 

• He accepted the Treaty of Purandar after the humiliation (Option 1): The humiliation had the opposite effect: Shivaji turned against the arrangement, so claiming that he accepted the Treaty of Purandar after the Agra episode is wrong.

 

• He was appointed governor of the Deccan (Option 3): Aurangzeb never appointed him governor of the Deccan; he treated him as a rebel noble and put him under guard, so no such office or honour was conferred.

 

• He was crowned Chhatrapati at Agra fort (Option 4): The coronation took place at Raigarh in 1674, not at Agra Fort, which was the seat of the Mughal emperor and could never have hosted such a ceremony.

question:
Consider the following statements about Shivaji:

1. He was born at Shivneri in 1630.

2. He died of fever in 1680.

3. He was crowned Chhatrapati at Agra.

Which of the statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Shivaji was born at Shivneri fort in 1630 (शिवाजी का जन्म 1630 में शिवनेरी में और मृत्यु 1680 में हुई)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: he died of fever in 1680, and a war of succession broke out between his sons Shambhaji and Rajaram.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: his coronation as Chhatrapati was held in June 1674 at Raigarh fort, not at Agra, which was the Mughal capital where he had earlier been held captive.

 

• Both Shivneri and Raigarh are hill forts in Maharashtra, yet only the first witnessed his birth and only the second his coronation, a distinction examiners often use for mixed options.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The coronation made Raigarh the Maratha capital.

 

• Shivaji's lifespan was about 50 years, 1630 to 1680.

 

• His eldest son Sambhaji eventually won the succession struggle.

 

• The span 1630 to 1680 gives Shivaji a life of about fifty years.

 

• Statements about Shivaji's life are a frequent test pattern, with the false item usually swapping a place or a year.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): This combination includes statement 3 along with 2, but the coronation at Agra never happened; the ceremony was at Raigarh, and statement 1 on his birth is also valid, so omitting it is an error.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Pairing statements 1 and 3 accepts the false Agra coronation and rejects the correct death in fever in 1680, so it endorses a fact that is untrue while dropping a true one.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Including all three statements fails because the third is false; Shivaji was enthroned at Raigarh in 1674, while Agra was the place of his confinement in 1666 under Aurangzeb.

question:
Shivaji's wars made him a legendary figure mainly because of his successful resistance against which of the following powers?

I. The Mughal Empire

II. The Adil Shahi Sultanate of Bijapur
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shivaji's military exploits and successful resistance against both the Mughal Empire and the Adil Shahi Sultanate of Bijapur made him a legendary figure (मुगलों और बीजापुर दोनों के विरुद्ध संघर्ष से शिवाजी प्रसिद्ध हुए)

 

• Against Bijapur he captured forts like Torna and killed its general Afzal Khan in 1659, and against the Mughals he defeated Shaista Khan and later raided Surat.

 

• Both statements are therefore valid, and neither can be dropped.

 

• The two enemies were quite different in character: Bijapur was a regional Deccan sultanate whose power was already declining, while the Mughals were the major imperial power of North India led by Aurangzeb.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Adil Shahis ruled Bijapur from 1490 to 1686.

 

• Aurangzeb finally annexed Bijapur in 1686.

 

• Shivaji's father Shahaji had once served the Bijapur court.

 

• Bijapur's capture of 1686 came after Shivaji's death, from Aurangzeb's own campaign.

 

• The Maratha chief Shahaji, Shivaji's father, had served Bijapur earlier, which explains why the young Shivaji's first clashes occurred in the Bijapur frontier.

 

NOTE

 

• Only I (Option 1): Selecting only the Mughal Empire ignores the equally important struggle with Bijapur, where Shivaji began his rise by capturing forts and defeating Afzal Khan in the 1650s.

 

• Only II (Option 2): Selecting only Bijapur ignores the confrontation with Aurangzeb's army, including the defeat of Shaista Khan and the siege of Purandar, which made him known to the whole of India.

 

• Neither I nor II (Option 3): Rejecting both is absurd because the fight against these two powers is exactly what built his reputation as a founder of an independent kingdom in the Deccan.

question: After the death of Shivaji in 1680, a war of succession broke out between his sons. Who emerged victorious?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shambhaji.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After Shivaji died of fever in 1680, a succession struggle followed between his sons Shambhaji (Sambhaji) and Rajaram, and Shambhaji emerged victorious (शिवाजी के बाद उत्तराधिकार संघर्ष में संभाजी विजयी हुए)

 

• Sambhaji was Shivaji's eldest son and ruled the Maratha kingdom from 1680 to 1689.

 

• Rajaram, born of Shivaji's second wife, remained a rival claimant and later took over the leadership after Sambhaji's execution.

 

• The brothers represented two courts at Raigarh, with Rajaram's party led by his mother Soyarabai and ministers who disliked Sambhaji, but Sambhaji took control of the fort and secured the throne.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sambhaji's mother was Saibai, Shivaji's first wife.

 

• He was a scholar who authored Budhbhushan in Sanskrit.

 

• His reign was dominated by war against Aurangzeb, who came to the Deccan in 1681.

 

• Sambhaji was crowned formally at Raigarh in January 1681.

 

• Rajaram's mother Soyarabai was Shivaji's second wife, and she tried to place her son on the throne, which is the background to the quarrel.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajaram (Option 1): Rajaram was the half-brother who lost this contest in 1680; he became the leader only in 1689 after Sambhaji was killed, so he was not the immediate victor.

 

• Shahu (Option 2): Shahu was Sambhaji's son, not Shivaji's, and was only a child in 1680, so he could not have been a competitor in a succession struggle among Shivaji's sons.

 

• Shivaji II (Option 4): Shivaji II was the son of Rajaram and Tarabai, born around 1696, which means he was not even alive at the time of the dispute following the death of the founder in 1680.

question: Sambhaji, who ruled the Marathas from 1680 to 1689, was related to Shivaji as his:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Eldest son.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sambhaji was the eldest son of Shivaji and succeeded him as ruler of the Maratha kingdom in 1680 (संभाजी शिवाजी के ज्येष्ठ पुत्र थे और 1680 में उनके उत्तराधिकारी बने)

 

• His rule lasted until 1689, when he was captured and killed during the war with Aurangzeb.

 

• He was the father of Shahu, who later became Chhatrapati, which makes Shahu Shivaji's grandson and not his son.

 

• As the eldest son and heir, Sambhaji had already accompanied his father on several campaigns, and he ruled in a period when Aurangzeb himself moved to the Deccan, making the war more severe.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sambhaji was born in 1657 at Purandar.

 

• He spent part of his youth as a Mughal mansabdar under the Treaty of Purandar.

 

• His son Shahu (Shahuji) later became Chhatrapati after release from Mughal captivity.

 

• He captured Mughal outposts in Khandesh and Burhanpur's region in the early years of his rule.

 

NOTE

 

• Younger brother (Option 1): Sambhaji was never Shivaji's brother; Shivaji's half-brother Vyankoji ruled Thanjavur, and his own sons were Sambhaji and Rajaram.

 

• Grandson (Option 2): Grandson is incorrect because the grandson of Shivaji through Sambhaji was Shahu, whereas Sambhaji himself belonged to the generation directly after the founder.

 

• Nephew (Option 3): Nephew would make him the son of a sibling of Shivaji, which contradicts the fact that his parents were Shivaji and his wife Saibai.

question: In 1689 Sambhaji was defeated by Aurangzeb's forces at Sangameshwar, which was followed by:
option_1: His killing and the arrest of his son Shahu
option_2: His victory and the capture of Bijapur
option_3: His escape to Gingee with his family
solution_text:
The correct answer is His killing and the arrest of his son Shahu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the 1689 fight at Sangameshwar Sambhaji was defeated by Aurangzeb, killed, and his son Shahu was arrested by the Mughals (1689 में संगमेश्वर में संभाजी पराजित हुए, मारे गए और शाहू बंदी बने)

 

• The capture of the Maratha ruler and his heir was a major success for Aurangzeb in the Deccan.

 

• Afterwards Rajaram, the son of Shivaji's second wife, took charge of the Marathas and carried the war on.

 

• The capture was a heavy blow for the Maratha side, because the ruler was removed in the middle of the war, and the Mughal strategy of the following years was aimed at eliminating the remaining centres of Maratha resistance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shahu remained a Mughal captive for about 18 years.

 

• He was treated as a royal hostage and was released in 1707.

 

• Aurangzeb had stayed in the Deccan from 1681 until his death in 1707.

 

• Raigarh itself fell to the Mughals in 1689 and Shahu with his mother was taken into their camp.

 

NOTE

 

• His victory and the capture of Bijapur (Option 2): Sambhaji lost, not won, at Sangameshwar, and Bijapur had already fallen to Aurangzeb in 1686, so no Maratha capture of that city occurred in 1689.

 

• His escape to Gingee with his family (Option 3): Rajaram, not Sambhaji, fled to Gingee, on the southeastern coast; Sambhaji was captured and put to death, so there was no flight with his family.

 

• His crowning at Raigarh (Option 4): Raigarh was the site of Shivaji's coronation in 1674, and Sambhaji had no coronation there after being defeated; the Mughals killed him in the very year of defeat.

question: Who took charge of the Maratha state after the death of Sambhaji in 1689?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajaram.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After Sambhaji's death in 1689, Rajaram, the son of Shivaji's second wife, took charge of the Marathas (संभाजी की मृत्यु के बाद शिवाजी की दूसरी पत्नी के पुत्र राजाराम ने कमान संभाली)

 

• His rule is dated from 1689 to 1700, and he led the resistance from the fortress of Gingee in the far south.

 

• Since Sambhaji's son Shahu was in Mughal captivity, Rajaram acted as the active head of the Maratha cause against Aurangzeb.

 

• The continuation of the struggle under Rajaram prevented the Mughal victory from becoming final, as the Maratha centre of resistance moved far away from the Mughal armies, to Gingee in the Tamil plain.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rajaram operated from Gingee fort in the Tamil country during the Mughal pressure on Maharashtra.

 

• He was also the husband of Tarabai.

 

• He died of disease in 1700.

 

• Rajaram escaped from Raigarh to Gingee in 1689-90 in disguise.

 

• The Mughal siege of Gingee lasted several years from 1690 and the fort fell in 1698, after which Rajaram moved back to Maharashtra.

 

NOTE

 

• Tarabai (Option 1): Tarabai was Rajaram's widow who became regent for her young son only after 1700, so she did not take charge immediately after Sambhaji's execution in 1689.

 

• Shahu (Option 2): Shahu had been arrested by the Mughals along with the fall of Sambhaji and spent years in captivity, so he was in no position to govern at that time.

 

• Balaji Vishwanath (Option 4): Balaji Vishwanath was an official who rose to prominence under Shahu and became the first Peshwa in 1713; he was not a ruler or claimant in 1689.

question: After the death of Rajaram in 1700, who ruled as regent for her minor son until 1707?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tarabai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After Rajaram died of disease in 1700, his widow Tarabai ruled as regent for her young son until 1707 (राजाराम की मृत्यु के बाद ताराबाई ने 1707 तक संरक्षिका के रूप में शासन किया)

 

• She continued the resistance against Aurangzeb and earned a reputation for energetic leadership in the Deccan.

 

• Her rule was challenged after 1707, when the Mughals released Shahu and a civil war broke out between the two claimants.

 

• Tarabai was Rajaram's widow, and she led the Maratha forces in the field against the Mughal army, so her regency was a period of active war rather than administration in peacetime.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tarabai's son was crowned as Shivaji II.

 

• She later established the Kolhapur line after losing to Shahu.

 

• Tarabai was the daughter of the Maratha commander Hambirrao Mohite.

 

• Her son, Shivaji II, was only about four years old at the time.

 

• Tarabai's regency is remembered for the survival of Maratha resistance in the Deccan until Aurangzeb's death, after which the Marathas recovered.

 

NOTE

 

• Jijabai (Option 2): Jijabai was Shivaji's mother and died in 1674, so she could not have been regent in 1700; the regent was Rajaram's widow, not the mother of the founder.

 

• Soyarabai (Option 3): Soyarabai was Shivaji's second wife and Rajaram's mother, and she was associated with the 1680 succession plot, not with the regency after Rajaram's death.

 

• Saibai (Option 4): Saibai was Shivaji's first wife and Sambhaji's mother, who died in 1659, long before this regency took place.

question: In 1707 Bahadur Shah I released Shahu from Mughal captivity, resulting in:
option_1: An alliance of Shahu with Aurangzeb
option_2: The immediate end of the Peshwa office
option_3: A civil war between Shahu and Tarabai
option_4: The annexation of Maharashtra by the Mughals
solution_text:
The correct answer is A civil war between Shahu and Tarabai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The release of Shahuji by Bahadur Shah I after Aurangzeb's death in 1707 led to a civil war between Shahu and Tarabai over the Maratha throne (शाहू की रिहाई के बाद शाहू और ताराबाई में गृहयुद्ध हुआ)

 

• Tarabai claimed the throne on behalf of her son, while Shahu claimed it as the son of Sambhaji.

 

• Through the support of Balaji Vishwanath, Shahu prevailed and became Chhatrapati, while Tarabai was sent to Kolhapur.

 

• The 1707 release was a calculated Mughal move meant to split the Marathas, since a freed Shahu could challenge Tarabai's authority, and it succeeded in producing a prolonged civil strife.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aurangzeb died in 1707 at Ahmednagar.

 

• Shahu won the Battle of Khed in 1707 against Tarabai's forces.

 

• Kolhapur became the seat of a separate Maratha branch from 1710.

 

• Shahu had spent his years in the Mughal camp, where he was educated in court manners.

 

• Mughal policy often relied on such releases of captives to divide opponents, and the strategy worked briefly by pushing the Marathas into a family conflict.

 

NOTE

 

• An alliance of Shahu with Aurangzeb (Option 1): Aurangzeb died in 1707, so an alliance with him was impossible, and Shahu was released by the next emperor, not by Aurangzeb, precisely to create rivalry among the Marathas.

 

• The immediate end of the Peshwa office (Option 2): The Peshwa office was strengthened, not ended, after Shahu's accession; Balaji Vishwanath became the first Peshwa in 1713 and real power moved to him.

 

• The annexation of Maharashtra by the Mughals (Option 4): The Mughals did not annex Maharashtra after 1707; they were weakened by the death of Aurangzeb and later lost their influence to the Marathas.

question: Because of the help of which Peshwa did Shahu become Chhatrapati, with Tarabai being sent to Kolhapur?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Balaji Vishwanath.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• It was because of Balaji Vishwanath that Shahu became Chhatrapati while Tarabai was sent to Kolhapur (बालाजी विश्वनाथ की सहायता से शाहू छत्रपति बने)

 

• Balaji Vishwanath was formally made Peshwa in 1713 and was the first of the hereditary Peshwas.

 

• From his time the Chhatrapati was a nominal king, and real power lay with the Peshwa.

 

• Balaji Vishwanath, a Chitpavan Brahmin from the Konkan, had worked as a revenue official and won Shahu's trust by supporting him in the war with Tarabai, and the reward was the Peshwaship.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• He is described as the second founder of the Maratha Empire.

 

• He served as Peshwa from 1713 to 1720.

 

• His son Baji Rao I succeeded him in 1720.

 

• The Kolhapur and Satara branches remained separate until the settlement of 1731.

 

• Tarabai's court at Kolhapur remained rival to the Satara court of Shahu, and the dispute was settled by the Treaty of Warna in 1731.

 

NOTE

 

• Baji Rao I (Option 1): Baji Rao I became Peshwa in 1720, after the civil war of 1707-1710 was long over, so he could not have secured Shahu's succession and Tarabai's removal.

 

• Balaji Baji Rao (Option 2): Balaji Baji Rao was the third Peshwa, ruling from 1740 to 1761, and he was not even in office when Shahu and Tarabai fought in 1707.

 

• Madhava Rao II (Option 3): Madhava Rao II belonged to the late eighteenth century, becoming Peshwa during the first Anglo-Maratha War, nearly seventy years after the Shahu-Tarabai conflict.

question: Balaji Vishwanath, the first Peshwa, is often described as:
option_1: The founder of the Maratha Empire
option_2: The second founder of the Maratha Empire
option_3: The last Peshwa of the Marathas
option_4: The leader at the Third Battle of Panipat
solution_text:
The correct answer is The second founder of the Maratha Empire.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Balaji Vishwanath, Peshwa from 1713 to 1720, is called the second founder of the Maratha Empire (बालाजी विश्वनाथ को मराठा साम्राज्य का दूसरा संस्थापक कहा जाता है)

 

• He was the first Peshwa, and after him the Chhatrapati was a nominal king while the Peshwa held real power.

 

• The first founder was Shivaji, who built the kingdom and was crowned in 1674.

 

• He rebuilt Maratha authority after the civil strife, bringing the sardars into the king's camp by granting them revenue rights, and so the Maratha state revived after the long war with Aurangzeb.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• He secured Maratha rights of chauth and sardeshmukhi through the Mughal court around 1719.

 

• The Peshwa office became hereditary in his family.

 

• He belonged to the Chitpavan Brahmin community.

 

• He died in 1720 and was succeeded by his son Baji Rao I.

 

• The reorganisation under him allowed the Maratha sardars to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi directly, which funded the later expansion of the state.

 

NOTE

 

• The founder of the Maratha Empire (Option 1): Shivaji, not Balaji Vishwanath, is regarded as the founder of the Maratha state; Balaji restored and reorganised it after the setbacks that followed Sambhaji's death.

 

• The last Peshwa of the Marathas (Option 3): The last Peshwa was Baji Rao II, who surrendered to the British in 1818, which makes him the final holder of the office, not its first.

 

• The leader at the Third Battle of Panipat (Option 4): The Marathas were led at Panipat in 1761 under the third Peshwa's reign, long after Balaji Vishwanath had died in 1720, so he played no part in that battle.

question: In the Maratha administration, the term 'Peshwa' denoted:
option_3: The Principal Minister or Prime Minister
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Principal Minister or Prime Minister.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Peshwa was the Principal Minister (Prime Minister) in the Maratha administration (पेशवा मराठा प्रशासन में प्रधानमंत्री होता था)

 

• Under Shivaji he led the Ashtapradhan council of eight ministers, and from 1713 the office became hereditary and dominant.

 

• After Balaji Vishwanath, real power rested with the Peshwa, and the Chhatrapati became a nominal head.

 

• Under Shivaji the Peshwa was merely the leading minister of eight and could be dismissed, but with the 1713 change the office turned hereditary and became the centre of the confederacy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word 'Peshwa' comes from Persian, meaning foremost.

 

• The Peshwa capital was Pune.

 

• The Peshwa office lasted from 1713 to 1818.

 

• The post of Peshwa under Shivaji was held first by Moropant Pingle.

 

• Peshwa literally means foremost in Persian, and the title was used for the chief minister of the Maratha king.

 

NOTE

 

• The commander of the army (Option 1): The army commander was the Senapati (Sarnobat), who was a separate member of the Ashtapradhan; the Peshwa was above him as chief executive minister.

 

• The collector of chauth (Option 2): Chauth was collected by Maratha officials and agents as a levy on neighbouring territories; the Peshwa was not just a tax collector but the head of the whole administration.

 

• The head of the judiciary (Option 4): The judicial head was the Nyayadhish, another Ashtapradhan minister dealing with justice, while the Peshwa handled overall administration and later political leadership.

question: Baji Rao I, who served as Peshwa from 1720 to 1740, was the son of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Balaji Vishwanath.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Baji Rao I (Peshwa 1720-40) was the son of the first Peshwa, Balaji Vishwanath (बाजीराव प्रथम बालाजी विश्वनाथ के पुत्र थे)

 

• He is popularly referred to as Baji Rao Ballal and is said to have fought 41 battles.

 

• His son Balaji Baji Rao, also called Nana Saheb, succeeded him as the third Peshwa in 1740.

 

• Baji Rao I's skill with mobile cavalry produced victories such as Palkhed (1728) over the Nizam, and Maratha armies under him moved quickly across Malwa and Gujarat, extending the state far beyond the Deccan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Baji Rao I is considered one of the finest cavalry generals in Indian history.

 

• He expanded Maratha power into Malwa and Gujarat.

 

• He signed the Treaty of Bhopal with the Nizam in 1738.

 

• Baji Rao I died in 1740 on the banks of the Narmada while on campaign.

 

• The Peshwa's military innovations stressed speed, with armies travelling light and living off the countryside, a practice that astonished the Mughal and Nizam forces.

 

NOTE

 

• Shahu (Option 2): Shahu was the Chhatrapati who appointed Baji Rao I as Peshwa; he was his patron and king, not his father, who was a Peshwa himself.

 

• Raghunath Rao (Option 3): Raghunath Rao was a later Peshwa-aspirant and the younger son of Baji Rao I, so he belonged to the next generation instead of being the father of Baji Rao.

 

• Balaji Baji Rao (Option 4): Balaji Baji Rao was Baji Rao I's own son and successor from 1740, so naming him as the father would invert the line of succession.

question: Which Peshwa, also known as Nana Saheb, ruled from 1740 to 1761?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Balaji Baji Rao.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Balaji Baji Rao, the third Peshwa, ruled from 1740 to 1761 and was also called Nana Saheb (बालाजी बाजीराव, जिन्हें नाना साहेब कहा गया, 1740-61 में पेशवा रहे)

 

• He succeeded his father Baji Rao I and presided over the Maratha empire at its greatest territorial extent.

 

• His tenure ended soon after the Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

 

• Under him the Maratha territory reached its widest extent, with armies in Bengal, Orissa, Punjab and Rajasthan, but the empire was loosely organised, which proved a weakness when it faced a united Afghan army.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• He is said to have died shortly after hearing of the Panipat defeat.

 

• He moved the Peshwa seat firmly to Pune and developed it.

 

• Do not confuse him with Nana Saheb of 1857, who was the adopted son of the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II.

 

• He is also remembered for developing Pune with new temples such as Parvati hill.

 

NOTE

 

• Balaji Vishwanath (Option 1): Balaji Vishwanath held office earlier, from 1713 to 1720, as the first Peshwa, so he was in no way the ruler during the mid-eighteenth century.

 

• Baji Rao I (Option 2): Baji Rao I governed in 1720-40 and is popularly known as Baji Rao Ballal, not Nana Saheb; he was the father of the person in the question.

 

• Madhava Rao II (Option 3): Madhava Rao II was the Peshwa recognised in the treaties of the first Anglo-Maratha war in the 1770s and 1780s, much later than the 1740-61 period.

question: The Marathas fought Ahmad Shah Abdali in the Third Battle of Panipat in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1761.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Third Battle of Panipat between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali was fought in 1761, during the Peshwaship of Balaji Baji Rao (1761 में पानीपत की तीसरी लड़ाई अब्दाली और मराठों के बीच)

 

• When Abdali invaded India, it became the responsibility of the Marathas to defend the country, and they fought bravely.

 

• The Maratha defeat checked their northward expansion and weakened the Peshwa's prestige.

 

• The Maratha army, which numbered tens of thousands including a large following of camp attendants, was defeated by Abdali's well-led forces, and thousands of soldiers died.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sadashivrao Bhau led the Maratha army at Panipat.

 

• Abdali was supported by Najib-ud-Daula and the Nawab of Awadh.

 

• The battle took place on 14 January 1761.

 

• Panipat is in Haryana and was the site of battles in 1526, 1556 and 1761.

 

• Afghan success at Panipat was largely due to heavy artillery fire from the Durrani side and the shortage of supplies among the Marathas.

 

NOTE

 

• 1739 (Option 1): The year 1739 is associated with Nadir Shah's invasion of India and the sack of Delhi, an event preceding the Maratha-Abdali contest by over two decades.

 

• 1757 (Option 2): The year 1757 saw the Battle of Plassey in Bengal, between Robert Clive and Siraj-ud-Daula, which is unrelated to the Maratha-Afghan struggle at Panipat.

 

• 1775 (Option 4): The year 1775 marks the beginning of the first Anglo-Maratha war with the Treaty of Surat, fourteen years after the Afghan encounter.

question:
Arrange the following Peshwas in chronological order of their rule:

A. Baji Rao I

B. Balaji Baji Rao

C. Balaji Vishwanath
solution_text:
The correct answer is C, A, B.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The chronological order is Balaji Vishwanath (1713-20), Baji Rao I (1720-40) and Balaji Baji Rao (1740-61) (पेशवाओं का क्रम: बालाजी विश्वनाथ, बाजीराव प्रथम, बालाजी बाजीराव)

 

• Balaji Vishwanath was the first Peshwa from 1713 and is called the second founder of the Maratha Empire.

 

• His son Baji Rao I followed him and fought about 41 battles, while Baji Rao's son Balaji Baji Rao, or Nana Saheb, was in office at Panipat in 1761.

 

• Balaji Vishwanath begins the list in 1713 and Balaji Baji Rao closes it before the Panipat disaster, so the three names cover the period of greatest rise of Peshwa power and expansion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Peshwa line was a hereditary succession in one Chitpavan family.

 

• After 1761 came Madhava Rao I, Narayan Rao, Raghunath Rao, Madhava Rao II and Baji Rao II.

 

• Baji Rao II was the last Peshwa, until 1818.

 

• Both Baji Rao I and Balaji Baji Rao were in office during Shahu's lifetime.

 

NOTE

 

• A, C, B (Option 1): This arrangement places Baji Rao I ahead of Balaji Vishwanath, but Baji Rao I was his son and succeeded him in 1720, so the father must come first.

 

• C, B, A (Option 3): Placing Balaji Vishwanath, then Balaji Baji Rao, then Baji Rao I reverses the last two; Baji Rao I ruled in 1720-40 and Balaji Baji Rao only from 1740 as his successor.

 

• B, A, C (Option 4): Beginning with Balaji Baji Rao is wrong since he was the third Peshwa, ruling in 1740-61, and so cannot precede both Balaji Vishwanath and Baji Rao I.

question: What was the collective name given to Shivaji's council of eight ministers?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ashtapradhan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shivaji's council of eight ministers was called the Ashtapradhan (शिवाजी के आठ मंत्रियों की परिषद अष्टप्रधान कहलाती थी)

 

• It included the Peshwa, Amatya, Sachiv, Mantri, Senapati, Sumant, Nyayadhish and Pandit Rao, each with a specific portfolio.

 

• The ministers were appointed by the king and acted as his advisers and heads of departments, not as hereditary nobles.

 

• The council was not a body of equals, as the king appointed each minister for his own department, and each of them was also expected to take military command when required.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Each minister was in charge of a department, and most of the posts were not hereditary under Shivaji.

 

• Ashtapradhan is derived from Sanskrit words ashta (eight) and pradhan (minister).

 

• Navratnas were the nine courtiers associated with rulers such as Akbar and Vikramaditya.

 

• Later the ministers' posts became hereditary under the Peshwas, unlike in Shivaji's time.

 

NOTE

 

• Navratna (Option 2): Navratna refers to a group of nine eminent courtiers, a concept linked with courts such as Akbar's, so it cannot be the eight-member Maratha ministerial council.

 

• Diwan-i-Khas (Option 3): Diwan-i-Khas was the hall of private audience in Mughal palaces like the Red Fort, a place for important meetings, and not a council of ministers under Shivaji.

 

• Mansabdari (Option 4): Mansabdari was the Mughal system of ranking officials by numerical grades, introduced under Akbar, and has no connection with Shivaji's ministerial structure.

question:
Match the Ashtapradhan minister with his function:

Column A: (a) Peshwa (b) Senapati (c) Nyayadhish (d) Sumant

Column B: (i) Chief of justice (ii) Prime Minister (iii) Foreign affairs (iv) Military commander
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Peshwa headed the Ashtapradhan as Prime Minister (a-ii), and the Senapati was the commander of the army (b-iv) (अष्टप्रधान में पेशवा प्रधानमंत्री और सेनापति सैन्य प्रमुख था)

 

• The Nyayadhish was in charge of justice (c-i), and the Sumant, also called Dabir, handled foreign affairs and diplomacy (d-iii).

 

• Together they show a division of tasks in the royal government of the Marathas.

 

• The role of the Sumant, or Dabir, included receiving envoys and handling communications with other courts, while the Senapati commanded the military forces, so each portfolio had a clearly defined area.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Amatya was the finance minister.

 

• Sachiv looked after royal correspondence.

 

• Pandit Rao was the minister for religious matters and charity, and Mantri dealt with the king's personal records.

 

• Nyayadhish and Pandit Rao were the only two ministers who were not expected to lead armies.

 

• The eight ministers were responsible to the king, who personally supervised the councils and remained the final authority in administration.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i (Option 1): This set swaps the Peshwa with the military role and the Senapati with the Prime Minister, which reverses two major portfolios, so the Senapati cannot be the Prime Minister.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 2): Pairing the Peshwa with justice and the Senapati with the chief of the army only partly fits; the Peshwa was Prime Minister and Nyayadhish was the justice minister, so it still misplaces a pair.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii (Option 3): Here the Peshwa is linked with foreign affairs and Sumant with Prime Minister, an inversion; Sumant was the foreign-affairs minister and the Peshwa led the council.
